_readme: Plain-English articles for the Learn section. Keep each one general and factual; don't put manufacturer-specific numbers here (those belong in error-codes with a source). keywords are the everyday words riders type; they power the search. Run `node tools/build-learn.js` after editing.

articles.title: Hub motor
articles.what: A motor built into the center of the front or rear wheel.
articles.does: It turns the wheel directly. It's the most common motor on lower-priced and many direct-to-consumer e-bikes, and it works independently of the bike's gears.
symptoms: Clicking or grinding from the wheel hub
A wheel that's hard to turn with the power off
Assist that cuts in and out over bumps (often a loose motor cable)
checks: Look at the motor cable where it leaves the axle: it should be undamaged and plugged in fully.
Check the axle nuts are tight and the wheel sits straight in the frame.
care: Keep the axle nuts and torque washers tight.
Don't hose the hub directly when cleaning.
Removing a rear hub-motor wheel is harder than a normal wheel; ask a shop if you haven't done one.

articles.title: Mid-drive motor
articles.what: A motor mounted at the pedals, in the middle of the frame.
articles.does: It drives the chain, so it uses the bike's gears like your legs do. That makes it efficient on hills. Bosch, Shimano, Yamaha, Brose and Bafang's M-series are mid-drives.
symptoms: Faster chain and cassette wear than a regular bike
Grinding or knocking from the motor area
Assist that feels uneven when you pedal (often the torque sensor)
checks: Check the cranks are tight and don't wobble.
Listen for noise with the power off while turning the pedals backward.
care: Shift to an easier gear before stopping and before steep climbs; easing off the pedals as you shift is kinder to the chain.
Replace the chain before it wears the gears out.

articles.title: Torque sensor
articles.what: A sensor that measures how hard you push on the pedals.
articles.does: The harder you pedal, the more the motor helps, which feels natural and smooth. Most mid-drives and better hub-motor bikes have one.
symptoms: Assist that's weak, delayed or uneven
An error or warning right after switching on
checks: Switch on with your feet off the pedals; many systems calibrate the sensor at start-up.
If assist stays weak, note any error code and have it tested.
care: Avoid switching on with weight on the pedals.
Torque sensors aren't a home repair; a shop can test and calibrate them.

articles.title: Cadence sensor
articles.what: A sensor that detects whether, and how fast, the pedals are turning.
articles.does: Once it sees the pedals turning, the motor gives the amount of help set by the assist level, however hard you push. It's simple and common on hub-motor bikes, and often uses a ring of magnets behind the crank.
symptoms: Assist that starts late or not at all
Assist that keeps going briefly after you stop pedaling
checks: Look at the magnet ring behind the crank: it should be in place, not cracked, and close to the sensor.
Check the sensor's cable is plugged in.
care: Keep the magnet ring clean; a damaged ring is a cheap part a shop can swap.

articles.title: Motor controller
articles.what: The electronics that decide how much power goes from the battery to the motor.
articles.does: It reads the sensors, the throttle, the brake switches and your assist level, and sets the motor's power. On mid-drives it's built into the drive unit; on many hub-motor bikes it's a separate box on the frame.
symptoms: Motor stops but the display stays on
Error codes about communication or overcurrent
A burning smell or heat from the controller box
checks: Check the controller's plugs are fully connected and dry. Look; don't pull hard.
Any burning smell: stop, switch off and don't ride.
care: Keep water away from controller connectors.
Controllers aren't a home repair; changing one usually needs the right model and settings.

articles.title: Pedal assist
articles.what: The motor helping you while you pedal.
articles.does: You choose an assist level (often Eco, Tour, Sport, Turbo, or 1 to 5). Higher levels help more and use the battery faster. Class 1 and Class 3 e-bikes are pedal-assist only.
symptoms: No help even though the display is on
Help that stops at a certain speed (that's the legal limit for your bike's class)
checks: Make sure an assist level is selected, not OFF or 0.
Squeeze and release both brake levers; brake sensors cut the assist.
Look for an error code on the display.
care: Use lower assist levels on flat ground to save battery.

articles.title: Throttle
articles.what: A lever or twist grip that runs the motor without pedaling.
articles.does: Class 2 e-bikes have a throttle. Some bikes only let the throttle work after you start pedaling, or have a separate setting for it.
symptoms: Motor runs on its own or won't stop (stop riding and switch off)
checks: Let go and check the throttle springs back fully.
Look at the throttle cable for damage. Look; don't pull on it.
Check your manual: some throttles only work once you're moving.
care: Keep the throttle clean so it doesn't stick.
A sticking throttle is a safety problem; have it replaced.

articles.title: Brake motor cutoff
articles.what: Switches in the brake levers that turn the motor off while you brake.
articles.does: They stop the motor fighting the brakes. Many e-bikes have them, especially hub-motor bikes with throttles.
symptoms: Motor won't help at all, but the display is fine
checks: Squeeze and release each brake lever firmly; a lever that doesn't fully spring back keeps the motor off.
Check nothing is pressing on a lever, like a bag strap.
care: If a lever is bent or sticky, have it fixed; brakes come first.

articles.title: Watts and power rating
articles.what: How much power the motor puts out, in watts.
articles.does: Bikes list a nominal (continuous) rating and sometimes a much higher peak. U.S. federal rules and Florida law define an e-bike's motor as under 750 watts; well beyond that, a bike may not count as an e-bike at all.
care: Compare nominal watts, not peak, when shopping.
More watts isn't always better; torque and the sensor matter more for how a bike feels.

articles.title: Torque (Nm)
articles.what: How strongly the motor can twist the crank or wheel, in newton-meters.
articles.does: Torque is what gets you up hills and moving from a stop with a load. Mid-drives often list 50 to 90 Nm; a higher number helps most on hills and cargo bikes.
care: For hills or heavy loads, compare torque more than watts.

articles.title: Lithium-ion battery
articles.what: The rechargeable battery that powers the motor, made of many small cells joined together.
articles.does: It stores a lot of energy in a small, light pack. That's also why damaged, cheap or badly charged packs can catch fire.
symptoms: Bike switching off under load or on hills
Heat, swelling, leaking or a strange smell (a danger sign)
checks: Look for cracks, dents or swelling. Any of those, or heat or smell: stop and read battery safety.
Check it's clicked fully into its mount.
care: Use only the charger made for your battery.
Store and charge it out of the heat and away from exits.
Never open a battery pack.

articles.title: Battery management system (BMS)
articles.what: The electronics inside a battery pack that protect it.
articles.does: It stops the battery charging too far, draining too low, getting too hot or giving too much current, and balances the cells. When it acts, the battery can switch itself off suddenly.
symptoms: Bike shuts off suddenly, often on a hill or at low charge
Battery shows full on the charger but the bike reads empty
Battery won't charge after sitting empty a long time
checks: Charge it fully with its own charger.
Let a very hot or cold battery reach room temperature before charging.
care: Don't leave a battery fully empty for long; that's when protection can lock it out.
Never bypass or open a BMS; it's what keeps the pack from overheating.

articles.title: Voltage (V)
articles.what: The battery's electrical pressure, in volts.
articles.does: The battery, controller, motor and charger are all built for one voltage, such as 36V or 48V. Mixing parts made for different voltages can damage them or cause a fire.
care: Only use a battery and charger made for your bike's voltage and connector, and approved by the maker.

articles.title: Amp-hours (Ah)
articles.what: How much charge the battery holds, in amp-hours.
articles.does: On its own, Ah doesn't tell you the battery's energy; multiply by voltage to get watt-hours, which you can compare between bikes.

articles.title: Watt-hours (Wh) and range
articles.what: The total energy the battery holds: volts times amp-hours.
articles.does: A 48V, 14Ah battery holds about 672 Wh. Range depends on that plus your weight, hills, wind, tire pressure and assist level, so the same bike can go twice as far on Eco as on Turbo.
symptoms: Range much shorter than it used to be
checks: Check your tires are pumped up; soft tires cost range.
Try a lower assist level and see how far you get.
care: Expect range to shrink slowly as the battery ages.

articles.title: Battery charger
articles.what: The charger made for your battery's voltage, chemistry and connector.
articles.does: It charges the battery safely and stops when it's full. A charger that merely plugs in isn't necessarily safe for your battery; CPSC has warned against "universal" e-bike chargers.
symptoms: Light blinks or shows full straight away
checks: Try another wall outlet, not a power strip.
Check both ends of the cord are fully plugged in.
Blinking usually means a fault; check the charger's label or manual.
care: Use only the charger that came with the battery or a maker-approved replacement.
Charge where you can see it, not overnight while everyone's asleep.

articles.title: Battery connectors and contacts
articles.what: The metal contacts where the battery meets the bike, and the port where the charger plugs in.
articles.does: Dirt, water, corrosion or a loose fit here causes power cuts, charging problems and heat.
symptoms: Burn marks or melting (a danger sign)
checks: Switch off, remove the battery, and look at the contacts: clean, dry and straight. Look; don't poke.
Any burn marks or melting: stop using it and treat it as dangerous.
care: Keep connectors dry; let them dry fully before charging after rain.

articles.title: Battery aging
articles.what: Lithium-ion batteries slowly hold less charge as they age and get used.
articles.does: Heat, sitting fully charged or fully empty for long periods, and very hard use speed it up. Many batteries are rated for several hundred full charge cycles before noticeably losing capacity.
symptoms: Bike cuts out at what the display says is 20% or 30%
checks: A shop can test a battery's real capacity.
care: Store it partly charged in a cool place if you won't ride for weeks.
Avoid leaving it in a hot car or in the sun.

articles.title: Rain and water
articles.what: E-bikes handle rain, but water in the wrong places causes faults.
articles.does: Most are built to cope with riding in the rain. Submerging the motor or battery, or spraying with a pressure washer, can push water into connectors and electronics.
symptoms: Faults or errors after rain or washing
checks: Switch off and let the bike dry fully before charging.
If the motor or battery was submerged, don't charge or ride it; have it checked.
care: Wash with a bucket and sponge, not a pressure washer.
Take the battery out before washing if your bike allows it.

articles.title: Display
articles.what: The screen or light panel on the handlebar.
articles.does: It shows speed, battery level, assist level and error codes. On some bikes it also turns the system on and holds settings like wheel size and speed limit.
checks: Check the battery is charged and seated.
Look at the display's cable and plug for damage.
Write down any error code and look it up.
care: Keep it out of strong sun when parked if you can.

articles.title: Error codes
articles.what: Numbers or letters the display shows when the system detects a problem.
articles.does: Each maker has its own list, so the same number can mean different things on different bikes. Always look up a code for your exact motor system.
checks: Write down the exact code before switching off.
Switch off and on once. If it comes back, look it up and stop riding if it's a safety fault.

articles.title: Firmware
articles.what: The software inside the motor, display and battery.
articles.does: Makers release updates that fix bugs and sometimes change how the bike rides. Parts with mismatched software can show errors.
checks: Ask a shop or use the maker's app to check for updates.
care: Only install updates from the maker's own app or a shop.

articles.title: Speed sensor
articles.what: A sensor that reads how fast the wheel turns, usually from a magnet on a spoke or the brake rotor.
articles.does: The motor needs it to know your speed and stop assisting at the legal limit. If the signal is missing or odd, assist is reduced or cut.
checks: Check the magnet is still on the spoke or rotor and lines up with the sensor. Don't bend anything.
Check the sensor's cable is plugged in.
care: Knocked magnets are the most common cause; check after transporting the bike.

articles.title: Walk mode
articles.what: A setting that makes the motor push the bike slowly while you walk beside it.
articles.does: Handy on ramps and when walking a heavy bike home. How you turn it on differs by system; check your manual.
care: Only use it while walking with both hands on the bike.

articles.title: Hydraulic disc brakes
articles.what: Brakes that use fluid in a sealed hose to push pads onto a metal rotor.
articles.does: They're strong and need little hand force, which suits heavier, faster e-bikes.
symptoms: Lever feels soft or spongy, or reaches the handlebar
checks: Squeeze each lever: it should feel firm and stop well short of the bar.
Soft or spongy: don't ride; the brake may need bleeding.
care: Keep oil and lube off the rotors and pads.
Brake bleeding needs the right fluid for your brand; a shop job for most riders.

articles.title: Brake pads
articles.what: The replaceable pads that grip the rotor.
articles.does: E-bikes wear pads faster than regular bikes because they're heavier and faster.
checks: Look into the caliper: if there's very little pad material left, have them replaced.
Grinding metal-on-metal: stop riding; that damages the rotor.
care: Pads contaminated with oil usually need replacing, not cleaning.

articles.title: Brake rotors
articles.what: The metal discs on the wheel hubs that the brake pads grip.
articles.does: Larger rotors brake better and cope with heat, which is why many e-bikes use them. Many rotors have their minimum thickness stamped on them.
checks: Look for bends or deep grooves.
Don't touch a rotor right after a long descent; it gets very hot.
care: Keep oil and lube off rotors.

articles.title: Chain
articles.what: The chain that carries your pedaling (and a mid-drive's power) to the rear wheel.
articles.does: E-bike chains, especially on mid-drives, wear faster than on regular bikes. A worn chain wears out the gears, which cost more to replace.
checks: A shop or a cheap chain checker tool can measure wear in seconds.
Turn the pedals backward and look for stiff links.
care: Clean and lube it regularly, more often after rain.
Replace it before it's worn enough to damage the gears.

articles.title: Derailleur and gears
articles.what: The mechanism that moves the chain between gears.
articles.does: Using the right gear saves battery and your knees. A bent derailleur or stretched cable causes poor shifting.
checks: Look at the derailleur from behind: it should hang straight down, not bent toward the wheel.
care: A bent derailleur hanger is common after a fall; a shop can straighten or replace it.

articles.title: Tire pressure
articles.what: How hard the tires are pumped up.
articles.does: The right pressure is printed on the tire's side as a range. Too low causes flats, wobbly handling and shorter range; fat tires run much lower pressures than road tires.
checks: Check pressure with a gauge at least every week or two.
care: Use a pump that fits your valve type (Schrader or Presta).

articles.title: Storing your battery
articles.what: How to keep a battery when you're not riding for a while.
articles.does: Heat and being stored completely full or completely empty are what age a battery fastest. Many makers suggest storing it partly charged in a cool, dry place; check your manual for its range.
checks: Check it every month or so and top it up if it's dropped low.
care: Not in a hot car, garage attic or direct sun.
Away from exits and things that burn.
Use the charger made for it when topping up.

articles.title: E-bike classes
articles.what: The three legal types of e-bike in Florida and most U.S. states.
articles.does: Class 1: pedal assist up to 20 mph. Class 2: throttle allowed, up to 20 mph. Class 3: pedal assist up to 28 mph. The class decides where you can ride, and local rules vary.
care: Check the class label on your bike.

articles.title: Maintenance schedule
articles.what: What to check and how often.
articles.does: Heavier, faster e-bikes wear tires, brakes and chains faster than regular bikes. Follow your bike maker's service intervals where they exist; the habits below are general guidance.
checks: Every ride: tires, brakes, battery charge (see the pre-ride check).
Every week or two: tire pressure, chain clean and lube.
Every few months, or sooner with heavy use: brake pads, bolts, wheel spokes, and a shop check-over.
care: Keep receipts and service records; warranty claims often ask for them.
